sections.h2: What does a quitclaim deed do in New Jersey?
sections.html:
A quitclaim deed hands over whatever interest the signer holds, and it promises nothing about that interest. The Division of Taxation describes it as a conveyance of only the right, title or interest the grantor has or may have, with no warranty that the grantor owns any particular title.

New Jersey cares about the wording. For the deed to count as a true quitclaim, it must say so in specific language, for example a sentence stating that the deed is called a Quitclaim Deed, that the grantor makes no promises about ownership and that the grantor simply transfers whatever interest exists. An attorney or title company cannot imply it. Because the deed carries no warranty, it suits transfers between people who already know the property's history, such as relatives or former co-owners, and it suits clearing up a possible claim on title. It is a poor fit when a buyer is paying market price and expects protection.

sections.h2: Is a New Jersey quitclaim deed exempt from the realty transfer fee?
sections.html:
No. The label does not create an exemption. The Division's fee FAQ warns that attorneys often move freehold interests in quitclaim format, and those transfers are taxable for realty transfer fee purposes. Whether a deed escapes the fee depends on the relationship and the facts, not on the form name.

The recording officer in the county collects the fee at the time the deed is offered for recording, in addition to normal recording charges. Anyone claiming a full or partial exemption must file an Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller, Form RTF-1, which is notarized and recorded with the deed. Ask the county clerk or register of deeds for the current recording charges, because those are county fees and are not set by the Division.

sections.h2: Which family transfers qualify for an exemption?
sections.html:
The exemption most families look for covers deeds between husband and wife, or between parent and child. The state's examples show how narrow it is.

Realty transfer fee treatment of common family deeds
TransferResult
Sale between parent and childExempt
Parent sells to daughter and her live-in boyfriendHalf of the price is exempt, half is taxable
Parent deeds to an adopted childFully exempt
Parent deeds to a stepchild who was not adoptedNot exempt
Parent places home in trust for the childrenNot exempt
Divorced spouse deeds a half interest under a settlement agreementNot exempt
Estate sale to a buyer not named in the willNot exempt

Source: NJ Division of Taxation, Realty Transfer Fee FAQs.

The divorce answer turns on a detail: a settlement agreement that is merely incorporated into a divorce judgment keeps its consensual character, so the exemption for a transfer made under a final judgment applies only when a judge orders the transfer.

sections.h2: What forms must go with a New Jersey deed?
sections.html:
A deed cannot be recorded without a Gross Income Tax form. N.J.S.A. 54A:8-9 requires a GIT/REP form for a transfer of real property, and the form is submitted at closing along with the RTF-1. The Division uses the forms to find out whether a nonresident seller must prepay estimated gross income tax on the transfer.

Family deeds get no special treatment here. The Division states there is no parent-to-child exemption for the GIT/REP requirements, so the seller's residency, whether the home is a principal residence, the consideration and any net proceeds are looked at the same way as in any other sale. For a nonresident who quitclaims property to a sibling or ex-spouse for $1,000 or less, the GIT/REP-3 with the box for consideration of $1,000 or less is used. Consideration includes open mortgages, so a deed that looks like a gift can still carry a taxable amount when a loan stays on the property.

sections.h2: Is there a 1 percent fee on larger transfers?
sections.html:
Yes, a 1 percent fee applies to the buyer when the total consideration is more than $1,000,000. People call it the mansion tax. The Division's FAQs explain that buying spouses cannot dodge it by signing separate contracts and receiving separate deeds, because the intent to buy one property together makes the combined price the consideration.

The 1 percent fee is not imposed when the buyer is an organization the IRS has determined to be exempt from federal income tax, or when the transfer meets New Jersey's exempt transaction rules. Most family quitclaim deeds fall far below the threshold, so this fee matters mainly for high-value property.

sections.h2: Where is a New Jersey deed recorded and what if it goes to the wrong county?
sections.html:
A New Jersey deed is recorded in the county where the land lies. After closing, the title agent or attorney usually files it. The Division's instruction for a deed recorded in the wrong county is to record it in the correct county, then file Form RTF-3 for a refund of the State portion and ask the wrong county's recording office for a refund of the county portion.

Because that mistake costs fees and time, confirm the county before signing.

sections.h2: When does a quitclaim deed make sense before a sale?
sections.html:
A quitclaim deed fits a limited set of situations in New Jersey, and it is not a shortcut around the tax rules.

  • adding or removing a relative from title when the exempt relationships above apply
  • releasing an ex-spouse's or co-heir's interest as part of an agreed buyout, with the fee calculated on the price plus the right share of any mortgage
  • confirming a name change on an entity's existing deed, which can be recorded without a transfer fee once the state certificate is on file
  • settling a possible claim on title before a buyer's title company reviews it

Where the goal is a sale to an outside buyer, a deed with warranties is normally what the buyer's lender and title agent expect. Talk with a New Jersey attorney or title agent before choosing the deed type.

faqs.q: Does a quitclaim deed remove my mortgage in New Jersey?
faqs.a: No. A quitclaim deed changes who holds the ownership interest, not what is owed on the loan. The Division counts open mortgage balances as consideration for fee purposes, so an unpaid mortgage can raise the realty transfer fee on a family deed.

faqs.q: Do I pay a transfer fee when I add my child to a New Jersey deed?
faqs.a: Often not for a parent and child, because a sale or deed between parent and child is an exempt transaction. A stepchild who was not adopted is not covered, and a transfer into a trust for the children is taxable.

faqs.q: Where do I record a quitclaim deed in New Jersey?
faqs.a: Record it with the county recording office for the county where the property sits. If it is recorded in the wrong county, record it again in the right one and apply for refunds using Form RTF-3 and the wrong county's refund process.

faqs.q: Is a quitclaim deed the same as a warranty deed?
faqs.a: No. A quitclaim passes only the interest the grantor has and makes no promise about title. New Jersey also requires specific wording for a deed to qualify as a true quitclaim.

faqs.q: Can a nonresident quitclaim a New Jersey property?
faqs.a: Yes, but a GIT/REP form is still needed to record the deed. A nonresident who conveys by quitclaim for $1,000 or less completes the GIT/REP-3 and checks the box for consideration of $1,000 or less.
